quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results (CEO Dave Regnery / CFO Chris Kuehn): 'exceptional enterprise organic bookings up 22%, driving a record backlog of $7.8 billion'; Q4 organic revenue grew 4% (7% excluding residential), led by Americas commercial HVAC and global services; 10% adjusted EPS growth. Americas commercial HVAC delivered record Q4 organic bookings, up more than 35% year over year, with revenue up low double digits and growth across nearly all verticals. Applied solutions bookings were up more than 120% with a record book-to-bill of 200%, 'marking the second consecutive quarter with applied bookings growth exceeding 100%'. EMEA commercial HVAC bookings up mid-teens (second straight quarter of mid-to-high-teens organic bookings growth). Residential revenue declined mid-teens as channel inventory was normalized (factory production days cut by one-third, roughly 60% deleverage in that business); China saw double-digit declines. Management said 2025 adjusted EPS exceeded guidance.
quarterly_data.figure: enterprise organic bookings up 22%; record backlog of $7.8 billion; Q4 organic revenue grew 4% (7% excluding residential); 10% adjusted EPS growth; Americas commercial HVAC bookings up more than 35%; applied bookings up more than 120%, book-to-bill of 200%

quarterly_data.signal: Backlog composition and visibility: 'Our commercial HVAC businesses in the Americas and EMEA added $1.3 billion in backlog versus year-end 2024'. Commercial HVAC backlog is up approximately 25% in the Americas and nearly 40% in EMEA, and 'the backlog is predominantly applied, which carries a long higher-margin services tail.' Of the $7.8 billion year-end 2025 backlog, management said 'there's a bit over a billion dollars of backlog that's for 2027 and beyond. That's up more than 30% versus a year ago, and it reflects multiple verticals.' Applied systems typically run about a nine-month cycle from order date to ship date, so second-half 2025 order strength (Americas commercial HVAC orders up over 30%, Europe up high teens) converts to revenue through 2026. CEO: pipelines in both businesses remain 'very, very robust' entering Q1 2026 after being the highest he had seen at the end of Q3.
quarterly_data.figure: $1.3 billion in backlog added vs year-end 2024 (Americas + EMEA commercial HVAC); backlog up approximately 25% (Americas) and nearly 40% (EMEA); a bit over a billion dollars of backlog for 2027 and beyond, up more than 30%

quarterly_data.signal: Initial FY2026 guidance (CFO Chris Kuehn): 6% to 7% organic revenue growth and adjusted EPS of $14.65 to $14.85 (growth of 12 to 14%); about 50 basis points from FX and roughly 200 basis points from M&A closed or committed for early 2026, for reported revenue growth of 8.5% to 9.5%; organic leverage of 25% or higher and free cash flow conversion of 100% or greater; pricing around a point and a half. Q1 2026: flattish organic revenue growth and adjusted EPS of approximately $2.5. The guide has Americas commercial HVAC up about 10% for the year, phased at roughly 7% to 8% in Q1, about 10% in Q2 and low teens in the second half, set by backlog and customer delivery timing. EMEA commercial HVAC expected mid-single-digit growth early, improving to high single digits in the second half as backlog converts. Residential flat to down up to 5% (Q1 the trough, down about 20%); transport flat to down low single digits against markets down high single digits (ACT forecasts Americas trailers down about 7% in 2026); Asia Pacific relatively flat. Transport and residential are 'around 25, 30% of the portfolio' with little growth assumed.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 organic revenue growth 6% to 7%; adjusted EPS $14.65 to $14.85; reported revenue growth 8.5% to 9.5%; Q1 adjusted EPS approximately $2.5; Americas commercial HVAC up about 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center architecture and future designs (CEO Dave Regnery, answering analyst questions on recent comments from a data-center partner about chillers and liquid cooling): 'we're working very closely with many influencers in the data center vertical. So think of hyperscalers, think of chip manufacturers, like Nvidia and others. We're helping them design data centers of the future. Or you may have heard them referred to as reference design data centers' - data centers to be built 'maybe two to four years out'. 'I have not seen a reference design or data center of the future that does not include chillers, just to be very clear', with 'a lot of innovation around the thermal management system, specifically around the chiller' in Trane's pipeline. Future data-center farms will build in free cooling: fans keep running through the free-cooling cycle while the compressor side runs less often; because chillers are sized to the thermal load, 'you're still gonna have the same number'. Asked whether HVAC's share of data-center spend is higher or lower two to four years out: 'I'm gonna err on the side of saying it's probably about the same', while 'the amount of power that is being consumed by the thermal management system may be less', letting operators redirect power to computing.

Data-center service economics (CEO Dave Regnery): 'hyperscalers or colos, they want the OEM to be doing the service work', and with very large data-center fields Trane is putting more dedicated resources on a single site; service attachment is far higher than a decade ago - 'I'd be hard-pressed to think where we've done a major chiller farm where we haven't had the service agreements.' The service tail on an applied thermal-management system is thought of at 'the eight to 10'; 'In data centers, look, to be honest with you, it's probably gonna be a bit lower', because compressor run-time may fall and more efficient chillers could be swapped out earlier to divert power to compute - still being modeled. Response time, uptime and connected solutions stay the same, 'So we'll still have a big robust service business.' Services are about one-third of enterprise revenue with a low-teens CAGR since 2020.
quarterly_data.figure: applied thermal-management service tail at the eight to 10 (data centers probably a bit lower); services about one-third of enterprise revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity for the applied ramp (CEO Dave Regnery / CFO Chris Kuehn): 'our chiller capacity over the last, you know, two or three years is up over four x', through new builds, lean work and new lines. Management also works with supply-chain partners on their capacity because 'their ability could hinder us if we're not careful' - 'we're in good shape there'. Trane commissions its applied systems with its own field force of over 7,500 technicians globally. Asked about capex, the CFO confirmed the analyst's capex-to-revenue range for the last few years ('You're right, Jeff') and said 'it's been able to support all the capacity expansions we needed to do', and that 'we brought in businesses on air handling or industrial process cooling capacity for data centers' via M&A, which adds capacity inside Trane's four walls. On lead times: no dramatic change for at least twelve months, Trane is 'very competitive on our lead times' and has introduced quick ship programs.
quarterly_data.figure: chiller capacity up over four x (last two or three years); over 7,500 technicians

quarterly_data.signal: Stellar Energy acquisition and capital deployment (CFO Chris Kuehn / CEO Dave Regnery): the largest acquisition, announced in December, is Stellar Energy, 'a leading provider of turnkey data center cooling solutions' with modular design-and-build capability for prefabricated cooling systems 'that ease supply chain and labor constraints and enable rapid scalable deployment'; expected to close in the first quarter with modest EPS accretion in 2026 after year-one acquisition and integration costs. Stellar builds modular chiller plants that 'get assembled on a job site like Legos', moving skilled labor and testing back to the factory; it is 'predominantly right now in the data center vertical', with 'some overlap' in customers and 'a lot of opportunities for this modular concept in core verticals as well'. In 2025 Trane deployed or committed approximately $3.2 billion (about $840 million dividends, $720 million M&A, roughly $1.5 billion share repurchases); for 2026 it expects to deploy between $2.8 billion and $3.3 billion, with $4.7 billion remaining under the repurchase authorization.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 deployed or committed approximately $3.2 billion ($720 million to M&A); 2026 deployment between $2.8 billion and $3.3 billion; $4.7 billion repurchase authorization remaining

quarterly_data.signal: Breadth and geography of demand (CEO Dave Regnery): 'we had 12 of 14 that were positive' among the Americas verticals tracked (life science was not), with data centers very strong alongside retail and office; the data-center vertical is 'almost all' new construction while core verticals skew to retrofit. 'We see data centers really on a global basis', but data centers being built in Europe are 'probably about, you know, one-tenth the size' of what is being built or planned in the US, and Asia is similar to Europe; the CEO is 'hearing from some that they're gonna be making much larger data centers in Europe', where Trane would be 'very well positioned'. Asked whether liquid-cooling-related orders are contributing, the CEO said revenue acceleration comes from orders already booked, and on 'robust demand for other elements of the thermal management system? Absolutely, certainly in our pipeline.'
quarterly_data.figure: 12 of 14 Americas verticals positive; European data centers about one-tenth the size of US builds

quarterly_data.signal: Input costs (CFO Chris Kuehn): tariff cost in 2025 was 'a bit higher than $140 million' after mitigation; the full-year wrap adds inflation 'maybe in that 50 ish million dollar range', and 'All in, maybe it's 200 ish million of cost that we'll make sure we price accordingly for', while working with suppliers to mitigate or move sourcing. About half of 2026 copper and aluminum needs are hedged, steel carries about a six-month price lock, and pricing will stay dynamic as commodities move. The Tier one raw-materials base is 'around $750 million' and Tier two 'around $5.5 to $6 billion'.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 tariff cost a bit higher than $140 million; 2026 tariff wrap 50 ish million; all-in 200 ish million of cost to price for; Tier one around $750 million, Tier two around $5.5 to $6 billion
